ar: Official or national language in over 20 countries across North Africa and the Middle East, the Arab world.
Modern Standard Arabic, used in writing and formal speech, differs widely from everyday spoken dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf and Maghrebi Arabic.
Written right-to-left in the Arabic script; it is the liturgical language of Islam and the language of the Quran.
Has given many loanwords to other languages, including Spanish, Swahili and Persian.
zgh: Covers a family of closely related varieties spoken across North Africa and the Sahara, including Kabyle (Algeria), Tashelhit and Tarifit (Morocco), and Tuareg (Sahel).
Co-official with Arabic in Morocco and Algeria since constitutional reforms in the 2000s–2010s.
Has its own ancient alphabet, Tifinagh, though Latin and Arabic scripts are also widely used today.
Spoken by indigenous Amazigh (Berber) peoples who predate the Arab conquest of North Africa.
am: The working/federal language of Ethiopia and native tongue of the Amhara people, centred on the Amhara region and Addis Ababa.
Written in the Ge'ez script, a unique syllabary also used for Tigrinya; it reads left to right.
A Semitic language despite being spoken deep in East Africa, related to Hebrew and Arabic.
Second most spoken Semitic language in the world after Arabic.
om: Most widely spoken native language in Ethiopia, the language of the Oromo people in the Oromia region surrounding Addis Ababa.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin-based Qubee alphabet since 1991.
Also spoken by Oromo communities in northern Kenya.
One of Ethiopia's federally recognised working languages alongside Amharic.
ti: Main language of Eritrea, the country's largest working language, and of Ethiopia's Tigray region.
Written in the Ge'ez script, shared with Amharic and Tigre.
Closely related to Tigre and more distantly to Amharic; it descends from the ancient Semitic language Ge'ez.
The 1998–2000 and 2020–2022 Ethiopia–Eritrea/Tigray conflicts were fought largely in Tigrinya-speaking areas.
so: National language of Somalia and Somaliland, also spoken across the Somali-inhabited Horn of Africa in Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin alphabet (Somali script) adopted officially in 1972.
Has an unusually rich oral poetry tradition, sometimes called a 'nation of poets'.
One of the few African languages spoken natively by a single ethnic group across several modern state borders.
aa: Spoken by the Afar people across the arid Afar Triangle: the Afar Region of Ethiopia, Djibouti, and coastal Eritrea.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin alphabet; traditionally has no single standardized orthography across all regions.
The Afar Region of Ethiopia includes the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest and lowest places on Earth.
Co-official regional language alongside French and Arabic in Djibouti's administration.
tig: Spoken by the Tigre people mainly in the Gash-Barka and northern lowland regions of Eritrea.
A Semitic language closer to the ancient Ge'ez than Tigrinya or Amharic are, but not mutually intelligible with Tigrinya despite the similar name.
Traditionally written in the Ge'ez script; some communities also use Arabic script.
Most speakers are Muslim, unlike the mostly Christian Tigrinya speakers to the south.
sw: A Bantu language with heavy Arabic influence, native to the Swahili coast of Tanzania and Kenya, and a lingua franca across East Africa.
Official language of Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and the African Union; co-official in the DR Congo and Rwanda.
Developed as a trade language along the Indian Ocean coast through centuries of contact between Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab traders.
Written in the Latin alphabet today, though historically also in Arabic script (Kiswahili cha Kiarabu).
ha: Most widely spoken language of the Sahel, concentrated in northern Nigeria and southern Niger.
A Chadic branch of the Afroasiatic family; traditionally written in Ajami (Arabic script) as well as the Latin-based Boko alphabet.
Major lingua franca of West African trade, spoken as a second language far beyond its core states.
Kano, Nigeria's second-largest city, is the historic heart of Hausa culture and commerce.
yo: Spoken by the Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria, centred on Lagos, Ibadan and Oyo, with communities in Benin and Togo.
A tonal language with three pitch tones; small diacritic marks show the tones in writing.
Carried to the Americas by the slave trade, it shaped Afro-Caribbean religions such as Santería and Candomblé.
Has a rich tradition of oral praise poetry (oriki) and drum-based talking communication.
ig: Spoken by the Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria, centred on Anambra, Imo, Abia, Enugu and Ebonyi states.
A tonal language with numerous dialects; a standard literary form was developed in the 20th century.
The former short-lived state of Biafra (1967–1970) was based in Igbo-speaking territory.
Chinua Achebe, author of Things Fall Apart, was a native Igbo speaker and drew heavily on Igbo culture.
ff: Spoken by the Fula (Fulani) people, traditionally cattle-herding, scattered in communities across the Sahel from Senegal to Sudan — one of the widest ranges of any African language.
Largest single ethnic group in Guinea, centred on the Fouta Djallon highlands; also a large minority in Senegal, Mali, Nigeria and Cameroon.
Belongs to the Senegambian branch of Niger–Congo, related to Wolof and Serer, and has grammatical noun classes marked by consonant changes.
Historically written in Arabic-based Ajami script before the modern Latin alphabet.
wo: Native language of the Wolof people and the de facto lingua franca of Senegal, understood by around 90% of the population.
Also spoken in the Gambia and southern Mauritania.
Not Senegal's official language (that is French), but its most widely spoken, including in Dakar's street culture and music (mbalax).
Belongs to the Senegambian branch of Niger–Congo, related to Fula and Serer.
bm: National lingua franca of Mali, understood by most of the population even where it is not the first language.
Part of the Manding group of Mande languages, mutually intelligible with Dioula/Malinke across Mali, Guinea and Ivory Coast.
Traditionally also written in the N'Ko alphabet, invented in 1949 specifically for Manding languages.
Centred on Bamako and the Niger River heartland of southern Mali.
ak: Most widely spoken indigenous language of Ghana; Twi and Fante are its two main varieties.
Akwaaba, the Twi word for 'welcome', is widely recognised across Ghana.
A Kwa branch Niger–Congo language, tonal, written in a Latin-based alphabet since the 19th century.
The historic Ashanti Empire, centred on Kumasi, was an Akan-speaking kingdom.
ee: Spoken by the Ewe people across the Volta Region of Ghana, Togo, and southwestern Benin.
A tonal Kwa language with a tradition of drum-based talking and praise poetry similar to neighbouring Akan.
Shares part of its homeland with and is closely related to Fon, spoken mainly in Benin.
Written in a Latin-based alphabet standardized in the colonial period.
mos: Native language of the Mossi people, the largest ethnic group in Burkina Faso, and the country's most widely spoken language.
Centred on the old Mossi kingdoms and the capital Ouagadougou.
A Gur (Voltaic) branch Niger–Congo language, tonal, written in the Latin alphabet.
French remains Burkina Faso's official language, but Mooré is the common everyday lingua franca.
kr: Spoken around Lake Chad by the Kanuri people, centred on Borno State in northeastern Nigeria, the historic Kanem-Bornu Empire.
A Saharan branch Nilo-Saharan language, unrelated to its neighbouring Niger–Congo and Chadic languages.
Written both in a Latin-based orthography and in Arabic-derived Ajami script.
Kanem-Bornu was one of the oldest and longest-lived states in African history, lasting from roughly the 9th to the 19th century.
ln: A Bantu lingua franca of the Congo River basin, widely used in Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo's army, and popular Congolese music (soukous).
Also one of the national languages of the Republic of the Congo, across the river from Kinshasa.
Developed in the 19th century from a riverine trade language as colonial and missionary activity spread it widely.
One of four national languages of the DR Congo alongside Kikongo, Tshiluba and Swahili, French being the official language.
kg: Language of the historic Kingdom of Kongo, spoken around the Congo River mouth in western DR Congo, Angola's Cabinda/Zaire provinces, and the Republic of the Congo.
A Bantu language; its speakers' descendants, taken in the slave trade, carried Kikongo-derived words and traditions to the Americas (e.g. into Haitian Creole and Kumina in Jamaica).
One of the DR Congo's four recognised national languages.
Closely related to, but distinct from, Lingala, the other major lingua franca of the lower Congo River region.
lua: Also called Tshiluba, spoken by the Luba people of the Kasai region in south-central DR Congo.
One of the DR Congo's four national languages alongside Lingala, Kikongo and Swahili.
A Bantu language, tonal, used widely in Kananga and Mbuji-Mayi, major cities of the Kasai provinces.
The diamond-mining region of Kasai gives Tshiluba speakers an outsized role in the Congolese economy.
rw: National and official language of Rwanda, spoken by virtually the entire population regardless of ethnicity.
A Bantu language, nearly mutually intelligible with Kirundi, spoken just across the border in Burundi.
Also spoken by Rwandan communities in eastern DR Congo (North Kivu).
One of the few African languages with near-universal national monolingual coverage within its country.
rn: National and official language of Burundi, spoken by nearly the entire population.
A Bantu language, closely related to and largely mutually intelligible with Kinyarwanda across the border in Rwanda.
Tonal, with a complex noun-class system typical of Bantu languages.
Amahoro, meaning 'peace', is a common greeting and a frequent theme in post-conflict Burundian public life.
lg: Language of the Buganda kingdom, centred on the capital Kampala, and the most widely spoken local language in Uganda.
A Bantu language serving as an everyday lingua franca across much of southern and central Uganda, alongside the official English.
Buganda is Uganda's largest traditional kingdom, with its own king (Kabaka) still recognised as a cultural institution.
Noun classes and extensive vowel-length distinctions are characteristic features of its grammar.
ki: Largest single ethnic language of Kenya, spoken by the Kikuyu people of the Central region around Mount Kenya.
A Bantu language, closely related to Embu and Meru, the neighbouring peoples of the same highland area.
The Mau Mau uprising against British colonial rule in the 1950s was centred in Kikuyu-speaking areas.
Many of Kenya's post-independence political and business elite have come from the Kikuyu community.
luo: Spoken by the Luo people around Lake Victoria in western Kenya's Nyanza region, and across the lake in northern Tanzania.
A Nilotic language, unlike most of its Bantu-speaking Kenyan neighbours, reflecting Luo migration south from South Sudan centuries ago.
Has no grammatical tones for lexical meaning but uses them for grammar, unlike many Niger–Congo languages.
Barack Obama's father was a Luo speaker from western Kenya.
zu: Most widely spoken home language in South Africa, native to KwaZulu-Natal and the Zulu kingdom founded by Shaka in the early 19th century.
A Bantu language famous for its click consonants, borrowed from neighbouring Khoisan languages.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages, and widely understood as a second language across the country.
Sawubona, literally 'we see you', is a well-known Zulu greeting.
xh: Native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa; like Zulu, it borrows distinctive click consonants from Khoisan languages.
Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki were both native Xhosa speakers.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages, widely spoken in Cape Town and the Western Cape as well as the Eastern Cape.
Closely related to Zulu; the two are partly mutually intelligible.
af: Descended from 17th-century Dutch brought by settlers to the Cape, with influences from Khoisan, Malay, Portuguese and African languages.
Mutually intelligible to a large extent with Dutch, though with simplified grammar.
Widely spoken as a first language among both white Afrikaner and Cape Coloured communities, especially in the Western and Northern Cape.
Also an official and widely spoken language in neighbouring Namibia, a former South African territory.
st: National language of Lesotho, a kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, and also one of South Africa's 12 official languages.
Centred on South Africa's Free State province and the whole of Lesotho.
A Bantu language closely related to Tswana and Northern Sotho, with mutual intelligibility between them.
Lesotho's near-total ethnic homogeneity makes Sesotho one of Africa's most universally spoken national languages.
tn: National and majority language of Botswana, where almost all citizens speak it either as a first or second language.
Also official and spoken in South Africa's North West province, bordering Botswana.
A Bantu language closely related to Sotho and Northern Sotho (the Sotho-Tswana group).
English remains Botswana's official language of government, but Setswana dominates daily and cultural life.
nso: Also known as Sepedi, centred on South Africa's Limpopo province.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages and among the five most widely spoken.
A Bantu language of the Sotho-Tswana group, closely related to Southern Sotho and Tswana.
Named Sepedi after the historic Pedi kingdom, though the language covers several related Northern Sotho dialects.
ts: Spoken by the Tsonga people across South Africa's Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces and southern Mozambique.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages.
A Bantu language; called Changana in Mozambique, where it is a widely spoken trade language in the south.
Closely related to, but distinct from, the Shona languages spoken further north.
ss: National language of Eswatini (formerly Swaziland), one of Africa's last remaining monarchies.
Also one of South Africa's 12 official languages, spoken in Mpumalanga near the Eswatini border.
A Bantu language closely related to Zulu, with similar click consonants and grammar.
Nearly the entire population of Eswatini speaks siSwati as a first language.
sn: Most widely spoken home language of Zimbabwe, used across most of the country except the southwest.
A Bantu language, named after the Shona people; the medieval stone city of Great Zimbabwe was built by Shona-speaking ancestors.
Written in a Latin-based orthography standardized in the 20th century from several related dialects.
Also spoken by communities in Mozambique's Manica province, bordering Zimbabwe.
nd: Spoken in Matabeleland in southwestern Zimbabwe, centred on the city of Bulawayo.
A Bantu language closely related to Zulu; Ndebele groups migrated north from Zululand in the 19th century under Mzilikazi.
Distinct from the Southern Ndebele language spoken in South Africa's Mpumalanga province, though related.
One of Zimbabwe's 16 officially recognised languages, second in speakers only to Shona.
ny: National language of Malawi, spoken by the large majority of the population as mother tongue or lingua franca.
Known as Nyanja in Zambia and Mozambique, where it is also an important lingua franca.
A Bantu language with a well-developed literary tradition and its own radio broadcasting history dating to colonial times.
Named after the Chewa people, historically linked to the Maravi Empire around Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa).
bem: Most widely spoken Zambian language, centred on the Copperbelt and Northern provinces.
A Bantu language used widely as a lingua franca across Zambia's mining towns, beyond its home region.
English is Zambia's official language, but Bemba is one of several recognised regional languages used in media and schools.
Closely related to other Bantu languages of the wider Luba-Bemba cultural cluster spanning Zambia and southern DR Congo.
umb: Spoken by the Ovimbundu, Angola's largest ethnic group, centred on the central highlands around Huambo and Benguela.
A Bantu language; most speakers are also fluent in Portuguese, Angola's official language.
Historically tied to the Benguela highland kingdoms and 19th-century caravan trade routes to the coast.
Despite being the largest Angolan ethnic language by speaker numbers, it has no official status nationally.
mg: National language of Madagascar, remarkably an Austronesian language, not an African one, brought by seafarers from Borneo roughly 1,500–2,000 years ago.
Closely related to Ma'anyan, a language of southern Borneo, far across the Indian Ocean.
Written in the Latin alphabet since the 19th century, replacing an earlier Arabic-derived Sorabe script used on the island.
Shows later layers of Bantu, Arabic and French loanwords from later waves of contact.
sg: National language and lingua franca of the Central African Republic, spoken as a first or second language by nearly everyone.
A creole that developed from Ngbandi, a local Niger–Congo language, mixed through river trade along the Ubangi.
French remains the official language of government and higher education, but Sango dominates daily communication.
Despite being spoken natively by relatively few, it functions as a true national lingua franca across dozens of local ethnic languages.
kri: English-based creole that is the lingua franca of Sierra Leone, spoken as a first language mainly in and around Freetown.
Originated among freed and resettled slaves brought to Freetown from Britain, Nova Scotia and the Caribbean from 1787 onward.
Although spoken natively by a minority, it is understood by almost all Sierra Leoneans as a second language.
English remains the official language, but Krio is the dominant everyday spoken language across the country.
zh: Official language of China, Taiwan and one of Singapore's four official languages.
Based on the Beijing dialect; written with Chinese characters shared (with different styles) across varieties.
A tonal language: the same syllable means different things depending on pitch (four tones plus neutral).
Has more native speakers than any other language in the world.
yue: Spoken mainly in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau, and in many overseas Chinatowns.
Has six to nine tones, more than Mandarin, and keeps more sounds from Middle Chinese.
Written with traditional Chinese characters, plus extra characters for colloquial speech.
The main language of Cantopop and much of Hong Kong cinema.
wuu: Centred on Shanghai, Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, in the lower Yangtze delta.
Shanghainese, its best-known form, is a prestige city dialect within Wu.
Keeps voiced consonants lost in Mandarin, giving it a softer sound.
Not mutually intelligible with Mandarin despite sharing written characters.
nan: Spoken in Fujian province, across Taiwan (as Taiwanese Hokkien), and in Hainan dialects nearby.
Carried by emigrants to Southeast Asia, where it shaped Chinese communities in Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Also written with a Latin-based romanisation (Pe̍h-ōe-jī) alongside characters.
Preserves many Old Chinese pronunciations lost elsewhere.
hak: Named after the Hakka people, 'guest families' who migrated south within China over centuries.
Core areas are inland Jiangxi and Guangdong, with communities across Taiwan and overseas.
Not centred on one province the way other Chinese varieties are, reflecting a history of migration.
Closer in some features to older northern Chinese than to its Cantonese and Hokkien neighbours.
ja: The national language of Japan, spoken almost nowhere else as a native language.
Written with a mix of Chinese-derived kanji and two native syllabaries, hiragana and katakana.
Has distinct levels of politeness and formality built into its grammar.
Its origins are debated; it is not clearly related to Chinese or Korean.
ko: Spoken on the Korean peninsula, divided between North and South Korea.
Written with Hangul, a featural alphabet designed in the 15th century under King Sejong.
A language isolate by most classifications, with no firmly established relatives.
Uses an elaborate system of speech levels marking respect toward the listener.
vi: The national language of Vietnam, also spoken by large diaspora communities abroad.
A tonal language with six tones, written in a Latin alphabet with added diacritics (Quốc Ngữ).
Heavily influenced by Chinese vocabulary after a millennium of Chinese rule, despite being unrelated structurally.
Replaced Chinese characters and a Chinese-derived script (chữ Nôm) only in the 20th century.
th: The national language of Thailand, written in its own script derived from Khmer and ultimately Indian scripts.
A tonal language with five tones that change a word's meaning.
Closely related to Lao, with speakers often able to understand each other.
Has distinct pronoun and vocabulary choices depending on the speaker's social status and gender.
lo: The national language of Laos, closely related to and largely mutually intelligible with Thai.
Written in the Lao script, a Brahmic script related to Thai's.
More native speakers of Lao-related Isan dialects live across the border in northeast Thailand than in Laos itself.
A tonal language, with the number of tones varying by dialect.
km: The national language of Cambodia, carved on the temples of Angkor over a thousand years ago.
Unlike most neighbouring languages, Khmer is not tonal.
Written in the Khmer script, the longest alphabet in the world with over 70 letters.
Has borrowed extensively from Sanskrit and Pali through Buddhist and Hindu influence.
my: The official language of Myanmar, spoken by the Bamar majority and used as a lingua franca by other groups.
A tonal language written in a rounded script shared with Mon and Shan.
Related to Tibetan, far up the Sino-Tibetan family tree, though the two look nothing alike today.
Shan, Kachin, Karen and other minority languages remain widely spoken in Myanmar's border states.
ms: Official language of Malaysia and Brunei, and one of Singapore's four official languages.
Standard Indonesian is its own standardised form of the same Malay language family.
Was long the trade lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia, written historically in Jawi (Arabic-based) script.
Shares most grammar and core vocabulary with Indonesian, though vocabulary and spelling diverge in places.
id: The national language of Indonesia, a standardised form of Malay adopted at independence.
Serves as a unifying lingua franca across an archipelago with over 700 local languages.
Written in the Latin alphabet with straightforward, mostly phonetic spelling.
Most Indonesians grow up speaking a regional language at home and learn Indonesian at school.
jv: Spoken across central and eastern Java, home to more native speakers than any other language without national official status.
Has an elaborate system of speech levels used depending on the listener's age and status.
Traditionally written in its own Javanese script, though Latin script dominates today.
Not the national language of Indonesia, which is a standardised Malay instead.
su: Spoken in West Java and Banten, in the highlands around Bandung.
The second most-spoken home language of Indonesia after Javanese.
Once written in its own Sundanese script, now mostly in Latin letters.
Distinct from Javanese despite being a close geographic and linguistic neighbour.
tl: Spoken natively in Manila and the surrounding provinces of southern and central Luzon.
Standardised as Filipino, the national language of the Philippines, and taught nationwide.
Absorbed heavy Spanish and, more recently, English vocabulary.
The Philippines has over 180 languages; Tagalog speakers are a large plurality, not a majority.
ceb: Spoken across Cebu, Bohol, Negros Oriental, Leyte and much of northern and eastern Mindanao.
By some counts has more native speakers than Tagalog, though it has no official national status.
Also called Bisaya or Binisaya by its own speakers, one of several Visayan languages.
Closely related to, but distinct from, Hiligaynon and Waray, spoken in nearby islands.
hi: One of India's two national-level official languages, alongside English.
Centred on the 'Hindi belt' of north India: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and neighbours.
Written in Devanagari, shared with Sanskrit and Marathi.
Shares a largely common spoken grammar with Urdu, though the two use different scripts and formal vocabulary.
ur: The national language of Pakistan, though most Pakistanis speak Punjabi, Pashto, Sindhi or another language at home.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script, unlike its close relative Hindi which uses Devanagari.
Spoken daily in the home by a sizeable minority, especially in Pakistani cities like Karachi, and parts of north India.
Grammatically very close to Hindi; the two are often considered one spoken language with two literary traditions.
bn: The national language of Bangladesh and official language of the Indian state of West Bengal.
One of the most-spoken languages in the world, with speakers concentrated in the Bengal delta.
Its own 1952 language movement in East Pakistan helped lead to the creation of Bangladesh.
Uses the Bengali script, also used to write Assamese.
pa: Split by the 1947 partition of Punjab between India and Pakistan.
In India it is written in the Gurmukhi script, associated with Sikhism; in Pakistan, in a Perso-Arabic script, Shahmukhi.
Has more native speakers in Pakistan than in India, though it holds no national official status there.
A tonal language, unusual among Indo-Aryan languages.
mr: Official language of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai.
One of the oldest Indo-Aryan literary languages, with records going back over a thousand years.
Written in Devanagari, the same script used for Hindi and Sanskrit.
Has a rich tradition of saint-poetry and, more recently, Marathi cinema and theatre.
gu: Official language of Gujarat state in western India; Mahatma Gandhi's native language.
Its script dropped the horizontal headline found in Devanagari.
Carried worldwide by a large Gujarati trading and emigrant diaspora, especially in East Africa and the UK.
Closely related to Hindi and Rajasthani, within the Indo-Aryan family.
kn: Official language of Karnataka state, home to Bangalore.
A Dravidian language, unrelated to the Indo-Aryan languages of north India.
Has one of the oldest continuous literary traditions among Dravidian languages, dating back over 1,500 years.
Written in its own rounded script, related to Telugu's.
ml: Official language of Kerala state in southwestern India.
Split off from Tamil roughly a thousand years ago and developed its own script.
Its script contains among the largest number of letters of any Indian script.
Kerala has one of India's largest diaspora communities in the Gulf states, carrying Malayalam abroad.
te: Official language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, spoken around Hyderabad.
Has the most native speakers of any Dravidian language.
Nicknamed the 'Italian of the East' by colonial-era observers for its vowel-rich, melodic sound.
Written in its own rounded Telugu script, closely related to Kannada's.
ta: Official language of Tamil Nadu state in India and of Sri Lanka and Singapore.
One of the longest continuously used languages in the world, with literature going back over two thousand years.
Written in its own looping Tamil script.
Resisted Sanskrit influence more than most other Indian languages, keeping a largely native vocabulary.
or: Official language of Odisha state on India's east coast.
Written in its own rounded script, shaped historically by writing on palm leaves.
One of India's languages recognised as 'classical' for the age of its literature.
Closely related to Bengali and Assamese, its eastern Indo-Aryan neighbours.
as: Official language of Assam state in India's northeast.
The easternmost of the Indo-Aryan languages, bordering Tibeto-Burman and Tai languages.
Shares its script, with minor letter differences, with Bengali.
Has its own distinct sound, including a voiceless velar fricative absent from most Indian languages.
mai: Spoken in the Mithila region of northern Bihar, India, and the adjoining Madhesh plains of Nepal.
Recognised as one of Nepal's official provincial languages and listed among India's scheduled languages.
Long counted by India's census as a dialect of Hindi before gaining separate recognition in 2003.
Has its own classical literary tradition, including the poetry of Vidyapati.
bho: Spoken across western Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, often grouped with Hindi in censuses.
Carried by 19th-century indentured labourers to Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana and Suriname, where it is still spoken.
Famous for its own film industry, 'Bhojpuri cinema', based in Patna and Mumbai.
Closely related to, but distinct from, neighbouring Maithili and Awadhi.
ne: The official and most widely used language of Nepal, home to over 120 languages.
Also an official state language in the Indian state of Sikkim and widely spoken in Darjeeling.
Written in Devanagari, like Hindi and Sanskrit.
Spread historically with the Gorkha kingdom's expansion across the Himalayas.
si: The majority language of Sri Lanka, spoken mostly outside the Tamil-majority north and east.
An Indo-Aryan language isolated far south among Dravidian neighbours, reaching the island around the 5th century BCE.
Written in its own rounded Sinhala script, related to other Brahmic scripts.
Co-official with Tamil at the national level since Sri Lanka's constitution recognised both.
dv: The national language of the Maldives, the only Indo-Aryan language spoken entirely south of India.
Written right-to-left in Thaana, a unique script developed in the 16th-18th centuries.
Closely related to Sinhala of Sri Lanka, its nearest linguistic relative.
Has absorbed Arabic vocabulary through centuries of Islamic influence.
dz: The national language of Bhutan, named after the dzong fortress-monasteries where officials once governed.
Written in the Tibetan script, shared with Tibetan itself.
A Tibetic language, related to Tibetan but not mutually intelligible with it.
Only became Bhutan's standardised national language in the 1970s, alongside many other local languages.
sd: Spoken mainly in Sindh province, Pakistan, home to the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script in Pakistan, and in Devanagari by Sindhi Hindus in India.
An official provincial language of Sindh, though not a national-level official language of Pakistan.
Has one of the largest consonant inventories of any Indo-Aryan language, including implosive sounds.
bal: Spoken across Balochistan, split between Pakistan, Iran and a corner of Afghanistan.
A Northwestern Iranian language, related to Kurdish and Persian but not mutually intelligible with either.
Has no national official status in any of the three countries where it is spoken.
Traditionally has a strong oral epic and ballad tradition among Baloch tribes.
ps: Co-official language of Afghanistan alongside Dari, dominant in the south and east.
Also widely spoken across the border in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and former tribal areas.
The traditional language of the Pashtun people and of Pashtunwali tribal custom.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script with extra letters for sounds not found in Persian.
fa: Official language of Iran (as Farsi), Afghanistan (as Dari) and Tajikistan (as Tajik, in Cyrillic).
A classical language of poetry, home to Rumi, Hafez and Omar Khayyam.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script in Iran and Afghanistan, but in Cyrillic in Tajikistan.
Served for centuries as the literary and administrative language across much of Central and South Asia.
tg: The national language of Tajikistan, a form of Persian written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Mutually intelligible with Dari and Farsi despite the different scripts, a legacy of Soviet-era script reform.
Also spoken by a Tajik minority in northern Afghanistan.
Retains some older Persian vocabulary that has shifted meaning in modern Iranian Farsi.
ku: Spoken across a region straddling Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria known as Kurdistan.
Co-official, alongside Arabic, at the national level in Iraq, and official within the Kurdistan Region.
Written in a Latin-based alphabet in Turkey and Syria, and an Arabic-based one in Iraq and Iran.
Not a single uniform language but a group of related varieties, chiefly Kurmanji and Sorani.
tr: The national language of Turkey and one of the official languages of Cyprus.
Switched from a Perso-Arabic script to the Latin alphabet in a 1928 reform under Atatürk.
An agglutinative language, building long words by stacking suffixes onto a root.
Part of the Turkic family, related to Azerbaijani, Uzbek and other Central Asian languages.
az: The national language of Azerbaijan, written in the Latin alphabet since the 1990s.
More native speakers live in Iran's Azerbaijan provinces than in Azerbaijan itself.
Closely related to Turkish, with a good degree of mutual intelligibility.
Was written in Cyrillic during the Soviet period, before switching to Latin script.
uz: The national language of Uzbekistan, the most populous country in Central Asia.
Officially switching from Cyrillic to a Latin alphabet, a transition still in progress.
Has a significant Uzbek-speaking minority in northern Afghanistan.
A Turkic language with heavy historical borrowing from Persian, reflecting Silk Road contact.
kk: The national language of Kazakhstan, the largest country in Central Asia by area.
Still mainly written in Cyrillic, with a long-planned transition to Latin script underway.
A Kipchak Turkic language, closely related to Kyrgyz.
Historically tied to nomadic herding culture on the Central Asian steppe.
ky: The national language of Kyrgyzstan, a mountainous Central Asian country.
Written in the Cyrillic alphabet, introduced during the Soviet period.
Closely related to Kazakh, with speakers often able to understand each other.
Home to the Manas, one of the world's longest epic poems, traditionally recited from memory.
tk: The national language of Turkmenistan, one of the most sparsely populated countries in Central Asia.
An Oghuz Turkic language, closely related to Turkish and Azerbaijani.
Switched from Cyrillic to a Latin-based alphabet after independence in 1991.
Also spoken by a Turkmen minority in northern Afghanistan and northeastern Iran.
ug: Spoken by the Uyghur people, concentrated in the Xinjiang region of northwest China.
A Turkic language, unrelated to Mandarin Chinese, written in a modified Perso-Arabic script.
Not an official language of China at the national level, though it has regional use in Xinjiang.
Historically a language of the Silk Road oases of the Tarim Basin.
tt: The largest Turkic language of Russia, centred on Tatarstan on the Volga River.
Co-official with Russian within the Republic of Tatarstan, though not at the national level.
Written in Cyrillic since the Soviet period, after earlier use of Arabic and briefly Latin script.
Also widely spoken by Bashkirs and others in neighbouring Bashkortostan.
mn: The national language of Mongolia, written there in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Also spoken in China's Inner Mongolia, where the traditional vertical Mongolian script is still used.
A Mongolic language, a small family distinct from the neighbouring Turkic and Sino-Tibetan languages.
Historically the language of the Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan.
bo: Spoken across the Tibetan Plateau, chiefly in China's Xizang (Tibet) Autonomous Region.
Written in the Tibetan script, adapted from an Indian Brahmic script in the 7th century.
Tonal in some dialects, including Standard Tibetan (Lhasa dialect), unlike most other Tibetic varieties.
The liturgical language of Tibetan Buddhism, used well beyond the Tibetan Plateau itself.
ka: The national language of Georgia, in the South Caucasus.
Written in its own unique Georgian script, with no close relatives outside the Kartvelian family.
Not related to Indo-European, Turkic or Semitic languages despite its location at their crossroads.
Has a famously complex verb system with many prefixes and suffixes marking person and case.
hy: The national language of Armenia, forming its own branch of the Indo-European family.
Written in a unique 36-letter alphabet created around 405 CE by Mesrop Mashtots.
Split historically into Eastern Armenian (spoken in Armenia) and Western Armenian (spoken by the diaspora).
Armenia was among the first states to adopt Christianity, shaping centuries of Armenian literature.
he: The official language of Israel, written right-to-left in the Hebrew alphabet.
Revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 19th and 20th centuries after surviving mainly as a liturgical language.
A Semitic language, related to Arabic and Aramaic.
Also the language of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), composed over roughly a thousand years.
en: The most widely used language in the world as a first or second language, and the main language of international business, science and aviation.
A West Germanic language that originated in early medieval England, later reshaped by heavy borrowing from French and Latin.
Written with the Latin alphabet; spelling is notoriously irregular compared to pronunciation.
Official or widely used in dozens of former British and American territories, from Nigeria to India to the Philippines.
es: Official language in Spain and nearly all of mainland Latin America, plus Equatorial Guinea; around 500 million native speakers.
A Romance language descended from Vulgar Latin spoken on the Iberian Peninsula, spread worldwide by Spanish colonisation from the 16th century.
Written with the Latin alphabet; distinguishes between formal 'usted' and informal 'tú' for 'you'.
The second most spoken native language in the world after Mandarin, and a major minority language in the United States.
pt: Official language of Portugal, Brazil and several African and Asian countries, a legacy of the Portuguese maritime empire.
A Romance language that evolved from Galician-Latin in north-west Iberia before spreading worldwide from the 15th century.
Brazilian and European Portuguese differ noticeably in pronunciation and some vocabulary, though they share the same writing system.
More native speakers live in Brazil than in all other Portuguese-speaking countries combined.
fr: Official language of France and an official or administrative language across much of francophone sub-Saharan Africa, a legacy of French and Belgian colonial rule.
A Romance language descended from the Latin spoken in Roman Gaul, standardised from the medieval dialect of the Île-de-France.
One of the few languages with official status on every inhabited continent, and a working language of the UN, EU and African Union.
Population growth means more first-language French speakers now live in Africa than in France itself.
ru: The most widely spoken Slavic language and an official or widely used second language across most of the former Soviet Union.
An East Slavic language written in the Cyrillic alphabet, with a literary tradition shaped by writers like Pushkin and Tolstoy.
Has a complex case system with six grammatical cases and a distinction between perfective and imperfective verb aspects.
Remains a lingua franca in Central Asia and the Caucasus decades after the Soviet Union's dissolution.
de: Official language of Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein, one of four official languages of Switzerland, and co-official in Luxembourg and Belgium.
A West Germanic language with a system of three grammatical genders and four noun cases.
Standard German developed partly from Luther's 16th-century Bible translation, which helped unify many regional dialects.
Known for long compound nouns and a sentence structure that often places the verb at the end of a clause.
it: Official language of Italy and San Marino, and one of four official languages of Switzerland, mainly in Ticino.
The Romance language closest to Latin in vocabulary and sound, standardised from the Tuscan dialect of Dante and Florence.
Vatican City uses Italian for most everyday administration alongside Latin for official church documents.
Famous for its role in opera, classical music terminology and the visual arts.
nl: Official language of the Netherlands, Belgium (as Flemish, mainly in Flanders) and Suriname.
A West Germanic language closely related to German and English, with a simpler case system than German.
Known as 'Flemish' in Belgium, though it is essentially the same standard language with regional pronunciation differences.
Also official in the Dutch Caribbean territories of Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten, alongside Papiamento.
pl: Official language of Poland and the native language of nearly all its population.
A West Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet with added diacritics, such as ą, ę, ł and ż.
Has a famously dense consonant system, including clusters like sz, cz and rz.
Spoken by large Polish diaspora communities in the United States, United Kingdom and Germany.
uk: Official and national language of Ukraine, spoken by the large majority of the population.
An East Slavic language written in a Cyrillic alphabet distinct from Russian in several letters and sounds.
Closely related to Russian and Belarusian but mutually distinguishable, with its own long literary tradition.
Ukrainian identity and language became a central symbol of national resistance after Russia's 2022 invasion.
be: Co-official language of Belarus alongside Russian, though most Belarusians speak Russian in daily life.
An East Slavic language closely related to Ukrainian and Russian, written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Use of Belarusian declined sharply during the Soviet era and remains a minority home language today.
Belarusian-language media and schooling have become associated with political opposition in recent years.
ro: Official language of Romania and Moldova, where it is also called 'Moldovan'.
The only major Romance language in Eastern Europe, descended from the Latin of the Roman province of Dacia.
Retains some grammatical cases, unlike most other Romance languages, likely from contact with neighbouring Slavic languages.
Written in the Latin alphabet since the 19th century, replacing an earlier Cyrillic-based script.
el: Official language of Greece and Cyprus, with the longest continuously recorded history of any Indo-European language, over 3,000 years.
Written in its own Greek alphabet, the ancestor of both the Latin and Cyrillic scripts.
Modern Greek descends from Koine Greek, the common language of the Hellenistic world and the New Testament.
Contributed enormous amounts of scientific and technical vocabulary to English and other European languages.
cs: Official language of the Czech Republic, mutually intelligible to a large degree with Slovak.
A West Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet with diacritics such as č, š, ž and ř.
The ř sound, a raised alveolar trill, is considered one of the hardest sounds for learners to pronounce.
Closely tied to Slovak after nearly 75 years as a shared state (Czechoslovakia) until 1993.
sk: Official language of Slovakia, closely related to and largely mutually intelligible with Czech.
A West Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet with diacritics including ľ, ŕ and ô.
Slovak and Czech speakers could generally understand each other during the 20th-century union of Czechoslovakia.
Standardised relatively late, in the 19th century, based on central Slovak dialects.
hu: Official language of Hungary and a recognised minority language in several neighbouring countries with large Hungarian communities.
A Uralic language unrelated to its Indo-European neighbours, distantly related to Finnish and Estonian.
Famous for extensive noun cases (around 18) and vowel harmony rules.
Hungarian communities remain large in Transylvania (Romania), Slovakia, Serbia's Vojvodina and Ukraine's Zakarpattia.
sr: Official language of Serbia and one of three official languages of Bosnia and Herzegovina, alongside Bosnian and Croatian.
A South Slavic language written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts, almost interchangeably.
Mutually intelligible with Croatian and Bosnian; the three are often described as variants of one pluricentric language.
Also spoken as a minority language in Montenegro and in Serb-majority areas of northern Kosovo.
hr: Official language of Croatia and one of three official languages of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
A South Slavic language written exclusively in the Latin alphabet, unlike Serbian which also uses Cyrillic.
Mutually intelligible with Serbian and Bosnian, though standardised separately with distinct vocabulary choices.
Became Croatia's sole official language after independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
bs: Official language of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the mother tongue of its Bosniak Muslim majority community.
A South Slavic language, mutually intelligible with Serbian and Croatian, written in the Latin alphabet.
Contains more loanwords from Turkish and Arabic than Serbian or Croatian, reflecting centuries of Ottoman rule.
Also spoken by Bosniak minorities in the Sandžak region of Serbia and Montenegro.
sl: Official language of Slovenia, spoken by nearly all of its roughly two million people.
A South Slavic language notable for retaining the dual grammatical number, used for exactly two of something.
Written in the Latin alphabet, closely related to but not mutually intelligible with Croatian.
One of the smallest national languages in the EU to have had full official status since Slovenia joined in 2004.
mk: Official language of North Macedonia, written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
A South Slavic language closely related to Bulgarian, with which it shares a high degree of mutual intelligibility.
One of the few Slavic languages, like Bulgarian, to have lost most noun case endings under Balkan linguistic influence.
Recognition of Macedonian as a distinct language has at times been politically disputed by neighbouring Bulgaria.
bg: Official language of Bulgaria, and the first Slavic language to develop a standardised written form, in the 9th century.
The Cyrillic alphabet itself was devised for Old Church Slavonic, a liturgical ancestor of modern Bulgarian.
Unusually for a Slavic language, it has lost noun cases but developed a distinctive set of verb forms marking narrated versus witnessed events.
Closely related to Macedonian, with which it shares high mutual intelligibility.
sq: Official language of Albania and Kosovo, and a recognised minority language in North Macedonia and Montenegro.
Forms its own branch of the Indo-European family, with no other close living relatives.
Has two main dialect groups, Tosk (the basis of standard Albanian) and Gheg, spoken mainly in the north.
Written in the Latin alphabet since the early 20th century, after centuries of competing scripts.
lt: Official language of Lithuania, one of only two surviving Baltic languages along with Latvian.
Considered one of the most conservative living Indo-European languages, retaining many archaic features close to Proto-Indo-European.
Written in the Latin alphabet with distinctive letters like ą, ę, ė and ų.
Has a complex case system with seven grammatical cases and pitch accent.
lv: Official language of Latvia, one of only two living Baltic languages along with Lithuanian.
Closely related to Lithuanian but not mutually intelligible, both descending from a common Baltic ancestor.
Uses fixed stress on the first syllable and marks long and short vowels with macrons (ā, ē, ī, ū).
Became the sole state language again after Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
et: Official language of Estonia, closely related to Finnish and, more distantly, Hungarian.
A Finnic language with no grammatical gender and up to 14 noun cases, unrelated to neighbouring Indo-European languages.
Famous for very long vowel and consonant lengths that can change a word's meaning.
One of the smallest languages to serve as an official EU language, spoken by just over a million people.
fi: Official language of Finland alongside Swedish, spoken by the large majority of the population.
A Finnic language unrelated to its Scandinavian neighbours, more closely related to Estonian.
Known for very long agglutinative words built by adding suffixes, and 15 grammatical noun cases.
Has no grammatical gender and no articles like 'a' or 'the'.
sv: Official language of Sweden and, alongside Finnish, of Finland, where it is spoken by a historic minority.
A North Germanic language closely related to Danish and Norwegian, largely mutually intelligible with both.
Uses a pitch-accent system that can change the meaning of otherwise identical words.
The autonomous Finnish region of Åland is almost entirely Swedish-speaking.
no: Official language of Norway, with two official written standards: Bokmål (most widely used) and Nynorsk.
A North Germanic language largely mutually intelligible with Danish and Swedish.
Norway has no single enforced spoken standard, and strong regional dialects remain common and socially accepted.
Historically tied to Danish, which was the written language of Norway for centuries under Danish rule.
da: Official language of Denmark and co-official in the self-governing territories of Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
A North Germanic language known for soft, often swallowed consonants, which can make it hard for other Scandinavians to understand when spoken.
Largely mutually intelligible with Norwegian and Swedish in writing, less so when spoken aloud.
Danish spelling retains many silent letters reflecting older pronunciations.
is: Official language of Iceland, spoken by roughly 330,000 people.
A North Germanic language that has changed so little since Old Norse that Icelanders can still read medieval sagas largely unaided.
Retains four noun cases and grammatical gender, unlike most other modern Germanic languages.
Coins new words from Icelandic roots rather than borrowing foreign terms, such as 'sími' (thread) for telephone.
fo: Official language, alongside Danish, of the Faroe Islands, spoken by around 70,000-80,000 people.
A North Germanic language descended from Old Norse, closely related to Icelandic.
Was mainly a spoken language until a written standard was devised in the 19th century.
Its spelling reflects Old Norse etymology rather than modern pronunciation, much like Icelandic.
ga: First official language of Ireland (alongside English) and an official EU language, though English is the daily language for most Irish people.
A Celtic language surviving as a community language mainly in small Gaeltacht regions along the west coast, such as Donegal, Galway and Kerry.
Belongs to the Goidelic branch of Celtic, closely related to Scottish Gaelic and Manx.
Uses a system of initial consonant mutations that changes word beginnings depending on grammar.
cy: Official language of Wales, spoken as a first or additional language by around 20% of the Welsh population.
A Celtic language of the Brittonic branch, closely related to Breton and the extinct Cornish.
One of the strongest-surviving Celtic languages, supported by Welsh-medium schools and dedicated media.
Famous for long place names built from descriptive compounds, like Llanfairpwllgwyngyll.
gd: A Celtic language spoken mainly in the Outer Hebrides (Western Isles) and parts of the Scottish Highlands.
Closely related to Irish, both descending from Old Irish of the Goidelic branch of Celtic.
Has official recognition in Scotland and support through Gaelic-medium schools, though speaker numbers remain under 60,000.
Not to be confused with Scots, a separate Germanic language also spoken in Scotland.
br: A Celtic language spoken in Brittany, north-west France, with no official status at the national level.
The only Celtic language still spoken on the European mainland, brought by migrants from Britain in the early Middle Ages.
Closely related to Cornish and Welsh, part of the Brittonic branch of Celtic.
Speaker numbers fell sharply over the 20th century, though Breton-medium schools (Diwan) now support revival efforts.
eu: Spoken in the Basque Country of northern Spain and south-west France, with no known relatives among other languages.
A language isolate, unrelated to Spanish, French or any other Indo-European language, and likely pre-dating them in the region.
Co-official with Spanish in the Basque Autonomous Community and parts of Navarre.
Known for its complex verb system and ergative case marking, unlike neighbouring Romance languages.
ca: Sole official language of Andorra, and co-official in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and the Valencian Community (as Valencian) in Spain.
A Romance language closer to Occitan than to Spanish, despite its geographic position within Spain.
Has a strong modern literary and media tradition, including its own television channels and a thriving publishing industry.
Barcelona's metropolitan area holds the largest concentration of Catalan speakers.
gl: Co-official language, alongside Spanish, of the autonomous community of Galicia in north-west Spain.
A Romance language closely related to Portuguese; both descend from medieval Galician-Portuguese.
Spoken by roughly half of Galicia's population as a first language, mainly in rural areas.
Has its own standardised spelling distinct from Portuguese, despite the close historical relationship.
lb: National language of Luxembourg, alongside French and German, both also used in administration.
A West Germanic language derived from a Moselle Franconian dialect, closely related to German.
Only became a standardised, officially recognised national language in the late 20th century.
Most Luxembourgers are trilingual, switching between Luxembourgish, French and German in daily life.
mt: National language of Malta and the only Semitic language with official status in the European Union.
Descended from Siculo-Arabic, with heavy later borrowing from Italian, Sicilian and English.
The only Semitic language whose standard script is a Latin-based alphabet rather than Arabic or Hebrew letters.
English is also official in Malta, making most Maltese fluently bilingual.
rm: One of Switzerland's four national languages, spoken only in parts of the canton of Graubünden.
A Romance language descended from the Latin of the Roman province of Raetia, with several distinct written dialects.
Has fewer than 50,000 native speakers, making it one of the smallest officially recognised national languages in Europe.
A unified written standard, Rumantsch Grischun, was created in the 1980s to bridge its local dialects.
se: The most widely spoken of the Sami languages, used across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland.
A Uralic language related to Finnish and Estonian, unrelated to the Scandinavian languages spoken around it.
Has official regional status in parts of Norway, Sweden and Finland, used in schools and local administration.
Reindeer-herding culture has given it an unusually rich and specific vocabulary for snow, ice and reindeer.
kl: Official language of Greenland, spoken by the large majority of its roughly 56,000 inhabitants.
An Inuit language of the Eskimo-Aleut family, closely related to the Inuktitut languages of Canada.
Famous for extremely long, polysynthetic words built by stringing many suffixes onto a single root.
Replaced Danish as Greenland's sole official language in 2009 under its home-rule arrangements.
qu: Official language of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador alongside Spanish, spoken across the Andean highlands.
Was the administrative language of the Inca Empire, spread across the Andes centuries before Spanish arrived.
Not a single language but a family of closely related varieties, with Southern Quechua (Cusco-Collao) the most widely spoken.
Millions of Peruvians and Bolivians, especially in rural highland areas, use Quechua as their first language.
gn: Co-official language of Paraguay alongside Spanish, spoken and understood by the large majority of Paraguayans.
The most widely spoken indigenous language in the Americas that is not confined mainly to its own ethnic group.
Uses nasal vowels marked with a tilde, such as the ẹ in its own name 'Avañe'ẹ'.
Most Paraguayans are bilingual, often mixing Guarani and Spanish in everyday speech known as Jopará.
ay: Official language of Bolivia and Peru, spoken mainly on the high Andean plateau around Lake Titicaca.
Spoken by several million people across the Bolivian departments of La Paz and Oruro and in southern Peru.
Noted by linguists for a three-way evidential system marking how certain a speaker is about their statement.
Sometimes described, with debate, as encoding time in reverse of most languages, with the past 'in front'.
nah: The most widely spoken indigenous language of Mexico, with around 1.7 million speakers, mainly in central Mexico.
Was the language of the Aztec Empire, written before the Spanish conquest in its own pictographic script.
Has given many words to Spanish and English, including 'chocolate', 'tomato', 'avocado' and 'coyote'.
Today spoken in many mutually distinct regional varieties rather than one uniform standard.
yua: Spoken on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula (Yucatán, Quintana Roo and Campeche) and in northern Belize.
A Mayan language descended from the writing tradition of the Classic Maya civilisation, one of the few fully deciphered pre-Columbian scripts.
Has around 800,000 speakers, making it the second most spoken Mayan language after K'iche'.
Uses a set of glottalised ('ejective') consonants not found in Spanish, written with an apostrophe, such as k' and ts'.
quc: The most widely spoken Mayan language, used in the western highlands of Guatemala.
Became internationally known through the Popol Vuh, a 16th-century K'iche' mythological and historical narrative.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchú is a native K'iche' speaker and advocate for Maya rights.
Like other Mayan languages, it uses ejective ('glottalised') consonants marked with an apostrophe.
ht: Official language of Haiti, alongside French, and the first language of nearly the entire population.
A French-based creole that developed among enslaved Africans on the colonial plantations of Saint-Domingue.
Has its own standardised grammar and spelling, distinct from French despite most vocabulary deriving from it.
Unlike French, verbs do not conjugate for person or number, instead using separate tense and mood markers.
pap: Official language, alongside Dutch, of Aruba and Curaçao in the Dutch Caribbean.
A creole based mainly on Portuguese and Spanish, with substantial Dutch and some African and Arawak influence.
One of the few creole languages with official status and its own press, schools and parliamentary use.
Spelling differs slightly between Aruba (more Spanish-influenced) and Curaçao/Bonaire (more phonetic).
nv: Spoken on the Navajo Nation, which spans parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado in the south-western United States.
An Athabaskan language, related to languages spoken much further north in Alaska and north-western Canada.
Famous for its use by Navajo 'code talkers', who transmitted unbreakable military messages during the Second World War.
Has one of the largest numbers of native speakers of any indigenous language in the United States, though numbers are declining among younger generations.
iu: An official language of the Canadian territory of Nunavut, alongside English and French.
An Inuit language of the Eskimo-Aleut family, closely related to Greenlandic and Alaska's Inupiaq.
Traditionally written in a unique syllabic script, alongside the Latin alphabet in some regions.
Like other Inuit languages, it builds very long words through extensive use of suffixes rather than separate words.
haw: Official language of the US state of Hawaii, alongside English, after coming close to extinction in the 20th century.
A Polynesian language closely related to Māori, Tahitian and Samoan.
Revived through Hawaiian-language immersion schools since the 1980s after decades of suppression in public education.
Uses only 13 letters along with the ʻokina (glottal stop) and macrons marking long vowels.
mi: An official language of New Zealand, the language of its indigenous Māori people.
A Polynesian language closely related to Hawaiian, Tahitian and Cook Islands Māori.
Underwent a major revival from the 1980s through Māori-language preschools (kōhanga reo) and broadcasting.
Everyday Kiwi English now borrows Māori words freely, such as the greeting 'kia ora' and 'whānau' (family).
sm: Official language of Samoa and co-official, with English, in American Samoa.
A Polynesian language with one of the largest speaker populations in the Pacific, over half a million people.
Samoan society's communal 'fa'a Samoa' way of life is deeply embedded in the language's vocabulary and honorific speech levels.
Widely spoken among large Samoan diaspora communities in New Zealand and the United States.
to: Official language of the Kingdom of Tonga, alongside English.
A Polynesian language with a complex honorific system reflecting Tonga's traditional chiefly hierarchy.
Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never formally colonised, helping the language retain strong everyday use.
Closely related to Niuean, and more distantly to Samoan and other Polynesian languages.
fj: Official language of Fiji, spoken natively by the indigenous Fijian (iTaukei) population.
An Austronesian language of the Oceanic branch, related to other Pacific island languages though not Polynesian.
Fiji Hindi and English are also widely spoken, reflecting the country's large Indo-Fijian community.
The friendly greeting 'bula', meaning 'life' or 'hello', is one of the best-known Fijian words internationally.
tpi: An official language of Papua New Guinea and the country's most widely used lingua franca, bridging hundreds of indigenous languages.
An English-based creole, also drawing vocabulary from German, Portuguese and local Austronesian and Papuan languages.
Functions as a main language of parliament, media and much everyday communication across the country.
Words are often playfully transparent, such as 'maus gras' (moustache, literally 'mouth grass').
